messages.subject: information curve for partial items
parts:
Dear Phil,

Thanks for making such a wonderful R package. It has been very useful to me, and I am sure that others have found it tremendously useful also.

I am measuring a construct using three separate methods (each having 6 indicators). All participants completed all three methods, and one method is clearly regarded as the 'golden' method to measure the construct. I am interested in comparing the three methods using information curves. Therefore, I have all the items (from the three methods) to load on the same latent factor. I wonder if there is any way to show the information curves for items in each of the three methods? Even better, is there a way to superimpose the information curves of the three methods above each other, so that I can see how they compare with each other within one figure (just like what the total information curves look like in multi-group comparison)?

Your help is much appreciated!

Best,
Chester Kam

parts: Hi Chester,
On Wed, Sep 7, 2016 at 5:38 AM, <chest...@gmail.com> wrote:

Dear Phil,

Thanks for making such a wonderful R package. It has been very useful to me, and I am sure that others have found it tremendously useful also.

I am measuring a construct using three separate methods (each having 6 indicators), and I am interested in comparing the three methods using information curves.

Why information curves? These can be subject a good amount of sampling variability and therefore can lead to poor inferences. It would be better to set up a test comparing the parameter estimates directly via Wald or LR tests. Alternatively, if information really is what you want, you'd need to include the variaiblity in the curves somehow (e.g., non-parametric bootstrapping). 
 
Therefore, I have all the items (from the three methods) to load on the same latent factor. I wonder if there is any way to show the information curves for items in each of the three methods? Even better, is there a way to superimpose the information curves of the three methods above each other, so that I can see how they compare with each other within one figure?

It is possible to do both things, though again I'm a bit worried about the use of information curves here. Is there a particular hypothesis that you are trying to test?

Phil

Your help is much appreciated!

Best,
Chester Kam

Hi Phil,

Dear Phil,

Thanks for making such a wonderful R package. It has been very useful to me, and I am sure that others have found it tremendously useful also.

I am measuring a construct using three separate methods (each having 6 indicators), and I am interested in comparing the three methods using information curves.

Why information curves? These can be subject a good amount of sampling variability and therefore can lead to poor inferences. It would be better to set up a test comparing the parameter estimates directly via Wald or LR tests. Alternatively, if information really is what you want, you'd need to include the variaiblity in the curves somehow (e.g., non-parametric bootstrapping).

I guess you mean I can test the item difficulty/discrimination by fixing/relaxing parameter estimates via Wald or LR tests. Definitely, the other two methods (let's call them Methods A and B) are not as good as the golden method (Method G) in assessing the construct, and thus item discrimination should be lower in the two other methods (in comparison with those in the golden method).

Therefore, I have all the items (from the three methods) to load on the same latent factor. I wonder if there is any way to show the information curves for items in each of the three methods? Even better, is there a way to superimpose the information curves of the three methods above each other, so that I can see how they compare with each other within one figure?

It is possible to do both things, though again I'm a bit worried about the use of information curves here. Is there a particular hypothesis that you are trying to test?

I am having the hypothesis that method A should be better in assessing those participants at the higher level of the construct. In contrast, method B should be better in assessing those participants at the lower level of the construct. Therefore, I was thinking of comparing the information curve between Methods A and B, as well as comparing both of them with the info curve of the golden method. I am using the curve of the golden method as a standard/reference.

Instead/In addition of examining information curve, do you have better ideas of how to examine this hypothesis (e.g., comparing item difficulty)? Thanks!

Phil
 

Your help is much appreciated!

Best,
Chester Kam

messages.subject: Re: information curve for partial items
parts:
Dear Phil,

Thanks for your previous reply to my question a long time ago, and I have been thinking about superimposing the information curve between two methods lately. My hypothesis is that items using method A will be better in assessing a construct at a higher level, and items using method B will be better in assessing a construct at a lower level. Items from both method A and method B will load on the same construct. Is there a way to superimposing the two information curves (from two methods) on the same figure, so that I can check if my hypothesis is valid or not? Currently, I only know how to request information curves from all items related to Method A or from all items related to Method B separately. Much appreciate your help!

Best regards,
Chester

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: information curve for partial items
parts:
Sure, but you'd have to construct such plots manually since mirt doesn't do this out of the box. iteminfo() is likely what you want to inspect, though note that in general simply drawing the tracelines could be a little misleading if your sample size isn't sufficiently large due to the sampling variability of the curves. You might have to think of a way to generate sets of variability for the plot, such as via bootstrapping or parametric draws from the posterior distribution (mirt has functions to do both things) to include confidence intervals around the associated information functions. Something like what the following does:

library(mirt)
x <- mirt(Science, 1, SE=TRUE)
plot(x, type='info', MI=100)

HTH.


Phil
